facts.note: §49 (p13) and Appendix B (p30). The §49 phrasing 'two £13.000 million' reads on first pass as £26m of LOBOs but Appendix B is unambiguous at £13m total — two loans, TOGETHER £13m. April 2026 has now passed (we are writing 15 August 2026); whether the option was in fact called sits in the next Bury treasury paper (not in scope for this write-up). Across our library so far, 12 LOBO calls logged and NONE has ended with the council accepting the lender's proposed higher rate — Bath and NE Somerset (2 KBC), Kent (Dexia), Tameside (Dexia), York, Harrow, Staffordshire, Wolverhampton (3), plus several ahead at Newport (3) and Bridgend. The 56.40% probability is an adviser model output, not market-implied.

facts.note: The paper prints no loan-level PWLB schedule so no direct table-vs-table reconciliation is possible. Two soft ties: (1) our £303.7m at 31/3/26 slots inside the implied PWLB portion of §39's £370.5m total (£370.5m − £13m LOBO − ~£54m LA/temporary − 0 Other ≈ £303-304m); (2) our weighted 4.43% is within 2bp of the paper's average all-borrowing rate 4.45%, driven by PWLB dominance. Historic as-at reconciliation to Appendix B's 31/12/25 PWLB (£259.7m) does NOT tie from our file (our data shows £135.3m at that date) — the `bc-loans` Start field is not a reliable drawdown date, as EMAIL_TEMPLATE §7 flags. courses_named: PWLB break costs — mechanics & live calculator
officer.body:
Hi Neil,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country. Below are a few thoughts on the 2026/27 Treasury Management Strategy that Council approved on 25 February. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it.

A disclosure first: your paper publishes no loan-level PWLB schedule, so we can't sit our file next to a printed table the way we usually open. What does tie without dispute is your paragraph 21. The balance-sheet identity closes to the pound in every one of the five years — CFR less external borrowing less other long-term liabilities equals your Under/(Over) Borrowing, from £96.1m in 2024/25 down to £68.0m by 2028/29. That is a tighter set of forecasts than most we read. On PWLB itself, our current file for Bury shows 31 live loans at £303.7m of principal at 31 March 2026 at a weighted 4.43%, which sits inside your paragraph 39 forecast of £370.5m total borrowing at 4.45% (the residual being your two LOBOs and the LA / temporary book).

The reason we wrote is your paragraph 49. Your two LOBOs both have option dates during 2026/27, and Arlingclose put a 56.40% probability on one lender exercising the option in April 2026 — with your stated response that if it happens, you would repay rather than accept a higher rate. April 2026 has now passed and 48235 alone can't tell us what actually did happen; that will land in your next treasury paper. Worth noting, though: of the twelve LOBO calls we have logged across councils this summer, not one has ended with the council accepting the lender's proposed higher rate. Bath and NE Somerset's two KBC loans went to floating with six-monthly resets; Kent and Tameside had Dexia call and repay; York's lender called and York repaid; Harrow, Staffordshire and Wolverhampton's three separate calls all refused and exited. If your April call did happen and Bury did what paragraph 49 says, that puts you alongside the twelve; if it didn't happen, that too fits — lenders have been restrained through 2025 and 2026.

The other observation is your paragraph 37, where you wrote that the rate environment has now opened up opportunities to mature debt at a discount, where premiums used to make it uneconomic. On the DMO's premature repayment curve today (notice 314/26, PM fixing, 14 August), your 31 live PWLB loans price at a net discount of about £2.4m — five sit below par, with the largest three on PW499634 (2037 maturity, 3.44%, £26m), 499389 (2032, 2.45%, £20m) and PW499636 (2032, 3.30%, £26m). Small in relative terms (about 0.8% of principal), but the pool you described does exist. Standard caveats and we mean them: we don't sell treasury products, we model no MRP or accounting treatment, only the DMO can quote a real settlement, and whether repayment is worth doing turns on replacement cost we can't see from here. Yours is at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis, updated daily.

The monthly PWLB draw breakdown and the daily LA-to-LA rate path sit at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity — it's how you can see thin weeks coming.

On training, three fit Bury. LOBO loans (legacy) is directly on point given your two options in 2026/27. PWLB break costs — mechanics & live calculator for the discount analysis. Debt restructuring for paragraph 52's history of using discount windows to reshape the book. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
https://www.linkedin.com/in/russelltew

Source: 2026-27 Treasury Management Strategy Report (Appendix 2), Council 25 February 2026 — https://councildecisions.bury.gov.uk/documents/s48235/appendix-2-2026-27-treasury-management-strategy.pdf.
